questions_json.explanation: The cocktail party effect shows that even when we focus on one conversation, our attention still monitors the background for personally meaningful signals like our own name.
options: Selective attention filters noise but still tracks personally important information like your name
Her hearing must be damaged by the loud music
Divided attention always improves memory
Sensory adaptation made the strangers' voices louder
questions_json.q: Sara is at a loud wedding, chatting with her friend. Suddenly she hears her own name mentioned by strangers across the hall, even though she was not listening to them. What does this demonstrate?

questions_json.explanation: Miller found working memory holds about 7 (plus or minus 2) items. Chunking groups digits into meaningful units, so more information fits into the same limited space.
options: Chunking removes the need to pay attention
Numbers are stored in long-term memory automatically
Chunking groups information into meaningful units, so limited working memory can hold more
Long numbers are naturally easier to remember than short ones
questions_json.q: Ali must remember the number 03017654321. He groups it as 0301-765-4321 and recalls it easily. Why does this trick work?

questions_json.explanation: Retroactive interference happens when newly learned information (Spanish) blocks the recall of older information (French).
options: Encoding failure — he never really learned French
Retroactive interference — new learning disrupts recall of older learning
Decay — his French memories simply faded away
Motivated forgetting — he unconsciously wants to forget French
questions_json.q: Bilal learned French for years, then started learning Spanish. Now he keeps mixing Spanish words into his French sentences. What is happening?

questions_json.explanation: Loftus demonstrated the misinformation effect: leading words like 'smashed' and suggestive questions can plant details that were never there.
options: Her memory naturally decayed over time
She has photographic memory that added details
Stress improved her memory accuracy
Leading questions planted a false memory — the misinformation effect
questions_json.q: After a car accident, a witness is asked: 'How fast was the car going when it smashed into the tree?' Later she clearly remembers broken glass, but there was none. What explains this?

questions_json.explanation: Confirmation bias is the habit of seeking, noticing, and remembering only information that supports what we already believe.
options: Hindsight bias — thinking she knew it all along
Confirmation bias — seeking only information that supports her existing belief
Anchoring bias — relying on the first number she saw
The availability heuristic
questions_json.q: Hina believes a new diet works. She only reads success stories about it and ignores every article showing it fails. Which bias is she showing?

questions_json.explanation: Functional fixedness is seeing an object only in its familiar role, which blocks creative problem solving.
options: A mental set caused by past failures
The incubation effect working too slowly
Functional fixedness — seeing the shoe only in its usual role
He lacked an algorithm for hanging pictures
questions_json.q: A man needs to hang a picture but has no hammer. A heavy shoe sits nearby, yet it never occurs to him to use it. What blocked his solution?

questions_json.explanation: Sternberg's triarchic theory includes analytical intelligence (book smarts), creative intelligence (novel ideas), and practical intelligence — the street smarts for handling everyday real-world problems.
options: Practical intelligence — street smarts for everyday problem solving
Analytical intelligence — academic test-taking ability
Creative intelligence — inventing completely new products
Musical intelligence
questions_json.q: Ahmed scores average on IQ tests but runs a successful shop: he reads customers well, negotiates cleverly, and solves daily problems fast. In Sternberg's theory, which intelligence is strongest in him?

questions_json.explanation: Gestalt psychology holds that the brain organizes sensations into meaningful wholes — by grouping, closure, and figure-ground — so the whole differs from the sum of its parts.
options: Weber's law of just noticeable differences
Sensory adaptation to constant stimuli
Signal detection under uncertainty
Gestalt principles — the brain organizes random patterns into meaningful wholes
questions_json.q: Children see animal shapes in clouds and a face on the moon. Which perceptual principle explains organizing random patterns into meaningful wholes?

questions_json.explanation: Simons and Chabris showed that intense focus on one task can make people completely miss a surprising event right in front of their eyes.
options: Selective hearing of unexpected sounds
Inattentional blindness — focused attention makes us miss obvious unexpected events
Change blindness in long-term memory
Divided attention sharpening visual focus
questions_json.q: Viewers asked to count basketball passes in a video completely miss a person in a gorilla suit walking through the game. What does this famous study demonstrate?

questions_json.explanation: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve and the spacing effect show that distributed practice builds far stronger long-term memory than cramming the same total hours.
options: The crammer — massed practice strengthens memory most
Both equally — total study time was identical
The spaced learner — the spacing effect makes distributed practice far stronger for long-term memory
Neither — forgetting makes all studying useless
questions_json.q: Two students study the same chapter. One crams all night before the exam; the other studies 30 minutes daily for two weeks. Who remembers more a month later, and why?
